content.Content:
# Old School Gamer Blog

* * *

## Ramblings from old-school gamers

Home Tools Blog Staff

# Hex Gen - Gygax Challenge

25 Jul 2025 \- Cpt. Redbeard

I’m planning on starting an Old School Essentials game and needed to create a
hex map for it. While looking up techniques to do this I came across this
video series by Games from the Front that inspired me to use this approach and
wanted to share it with my fellow TTRPG enthusiasts: Old School Essentials.

This approach can be used for any OSR (Old School Renaissance or Old School
Revival) game like the original AD&D Dungeon Master’s Guide (DMG) 1e, Dungeon
Crawl Classics (DCC), Shadowdark, Deathbringer, Grave, Iron Halberd, Knave,
Basic Fantasy, and many others based on the original DnD rules.

The main inspiration for this “world building” process comes from The Gygax 75
Challenge that suggests the following steps:

  1. The Concept: Pitch -> Sources of Inspiration
  2. Surrounding Area
  3. The Dungeon
  4. Town Features
  5. The Larger World

# Week 1: The Concept: Pitch and Sources of Inspiration

So to get started, you need to articulate the big ideas and gather sources.

> “Step 1 is something you do in your head. Now, fantasy/swords & sorcery
> games need not have any fixed basis for the assumptions made by its referee
> (my own doesn’t) except those which embrace the whole of fantasy. This sort
> of campaign can mix any and all of the various bases which will be mentioned
> below - and then some. […] Settings based upon limits (if one can speak of
> fantasy limits) can be very interesting in themselves providing the scope of
> the setting will allow the players relative free-reign to their
> imaginations.” – E.G.G.

## Pitch

In the Gygax 75 Challenge is suggested that you write down 3-7 well-crafted
bullet points that will both communicate and “sell” the world to your players.

For example:

  * _The Forsaken Frontier_ is on the edge of civilization where settlers seek their fortune and cling to the protection of local nobles and warlords.
  * _The Wilds._ Not far beyond though, the Frontier is wild where millennia of forgotten civilizations lie in ruins crawling with monsters, evil sorcerers, distant kingdoms of ancient races, and in the unexplored depths an otherworldly evil.
  * _Player characters are human._ Creatures that are either more or less than human come from interactions between gods and mortals or from a more ancient time. These creatures are feared and mistrusted, even if some have become human (e.g. the centaurs).
  * _Magic is unknown, dangerous, and inhuman._ Even the best wizards occasionally fail to properly harness a spell, with unpredictable results. Low-level wizards are powerful. High-level wizards fear for their souls. Continual use of magic results in…changes. Exposure to demons, radiation from other planes, elemental energies in toxic quantities, and the servants of Chaos all affect a wizard over the course of his career. Magic is unpredictable and spells can fail, or may misfire, and the magic user may suffer corruption.

## Sources of Inspiration

  * The Keep on the Borderlands and the Amber Castle, book series like The Legend of Drizzt by R.A. Salvatore and The Black Company by Glen Cook, and the classic AD&D 1e Dungeon Masters Guide.

# Tools

So, how do you go about creating your own hex map from scratch using the
random tables in the AD&D 1e Dungeon Masters Guide (DMG) and other resources?

I’m using the tool Worldgrapher because the pro version allows multiple map
levels so you can start with a high-level world map and zoom into continent,
kingdom, and province detail maps which works well with the DMG and can be
fully configured and customized to your preferred number of hexes within the
previous levels hex. I’ve also used the free version, Hexographer, for years
to create hex maps and will work fine for this you just have to create a
separate map for each level so the steps will be slightly different.

Filling in the Blanks and D30 Sandbox Companion have useful rules for
generating specific aspects of your world too that are useful.

* * *

# That's it, for now!

Check out the Blog for more posts!

  
  
\- Back to Top -

content.Subtitle: Once you’ve got your concept and pitch figured out you’ll need to start creating your hex map, one settlement of significant size where your players start out (e.g. The Village of Hommlet), at least 2 other settlements, other major terrain feature, a mysterious site to explore (e.g. The Moathouse), a dungeon entrance, and a random encounter table for the area.
content.Content:
# Old School Gamer Blog

* * *

## Ramblings from old-school gamers

Home Tools Blog Staff

# Hex Gen - The Surrounding Area

26 Jul 2025 \- Cpt. Redbeard

Once you’ve got your concept and pitch figured out you’ll need to start
creating your hex map, one settlement of significant size where your players
start out (e.g. The Village of Hommlet), at least 2 other settlements, other
major terrain feature, a mysterious site to explore (e.g. The Moathouse), a
dungeon entrance, and a random encounter table for the area.

> ”[…] sitting down with a large piece of hex ruled paper and drawing a large
> scale map. A map with a scale of 1 hex = 1 mile will be about right for
> player operations such as exploring, camping, adventuring, and eventually
> building their strongholds. Even such small things as a witch’s hut and side
> entrances to the dungeon can be shown on the map. The central features of
> the map must be the major town and the dungeon entrance.” – E.G.G.

## Set up Worldographer

Here’s the steps to setup Worldgrapher for a 15x15 hex map at the WORLD level:

  1. Open Worldographer
  2. Select File->New World/Kingdom Map
  3. Settings:

     * _Hexes Wide:_ 15
     * _Hexes High:_ 15
     * _Initial View Level:_ WORLD
     * Select _All one terrain_ and set to: Blank

  1. Click **Generate Map**
  2. Add label at World Level with the text “30mi/hex” by selecting Label->New Text Label and clicking on the the map to place it. Make sure only World is checked else it’ll appear on every level, not just the World level.

  

  1. Show hex numbers & reduce size:

     * Check _Numbers_ in bottom toolbar 
     * Click the cog icon to the right of Numbers to Configure Tile Numbers
     * Make a lighter _Color_ (e.g. #4d4d4d)
     * Set _Size_ to 12
     * Set _Pre-Pad_ to 10s digit

## Select Center Atlas-level Hex Terrain

Note: Atlas-level = WORLD level in Worldographer

Here’s the steps to set the starting location on the World map (known as
Atlas-level map in AD&D) for your **One large settlement** (define large
however you like):

  1. Select Terrain->Farmland (aka plains in DMG) & click on starting hex, e.g. 08.05, where the campaign will begin

  1. Select Feature->Building Clanmoot icon (if you right-click on the icon or terrain you can add it to your favorites so easy to find again)
  2. Enter label, e.g. Village of Hommlet
  3. Settings:

     * Check _Override color_ and set to appropriate color e.g. Black
     * Check _Override Default Scale_ and set to appropriate scale, e.g. 75
     * Check _Scale height independently_ and set to appropriate scale, e.g. 75
     * Set _Label Style_ to City or Village
     * Make sure World, Continent, Kingdom and Province is checked so feature icon and label appears on every level of the map

  1. Click in starting hex to place feature icon & label for starting settlement, e.g. 08.05

## Generate Surroundings Atlas-level Hex Terrain

Use APPENDIX B: RANDOM WILDERNESS TERRAIN table on page 173 of the DMG to
generate terrain surrounding starting tile. For the Atlas-level that’s just 6
tiles.

The tool below allows you to select the starting tile terrain type, “Plains”
in this case, and then click the link in step 1 to randomly generating the
terrain types for the 6 surrounding tiles.

Here’s the steps to generate terrain:

  1. Roll a d20 6 times, noting down the result for each roll. These are the 6 terrain types surrounding your starting hex.
  2. Define the terrain type for each roll using the table below by matching the result under your starting tile’s terrain column, i.e. Plains, with the terrain type, e.g. if you rolled a 12 it is Scrub
  3. Apply the generated terrains to surrounding hexes in Worldographer of starting hex, e.g. 08.06, starting at hex above, e.g. 08.04, and continuing clockwise for all 6 surrounding cells 
     * Depressions & Ponds: retains prior terrain type and apply special marking indicating it’s a depression or pond
     * 1 in 10 chance for Hills to include Forests and Forests to include Hills: roll a d10 for each hill and each forest hex to see if they contain both then update hex to represent that (link in step 1 automatically does this for you)

## Generate Terrain

Starting Tile: Plains Scrub Forest Desert Hills Mountains Marsh Rolls: Terrain
Types:

Re-roll

  
_Appendix B – Random Wilderness Terrain_

| Plains | Scrub | Forest | Rough | Desert | Hills | Mountains | Marsh  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
Plains | 1-11 | 1-3 | 1 | 1-2 | 1-3 | 1 | 1 | 1-2  
Scrub | 12 | 4-11 | 2-4 | 3-4 | 4-5 | 2-3 | 2 | 3-4  
Forest* | 13 | 12-13 | 12-14 | 5 | N/A | 4-5 | 3 | 5-6  
Rough | 14 | 14 | 15 | 6-8 | 6-8 | 6-7 | 4-5 | 7  
Desert | 15 | 15 | N/A | 9-10 | 9-14 | 8 | 6 | N/A  
Hills** | 16 | 16 | 16 | 11-15 | 15 | 9-14 | 7-10 | 8  
Mountains*** | 17 | 17 | 17 | 16-17 | 16-17 | 15-16 | 11-18 | N/A  
Marsh | 18 | 18 | 18 | 18 | 18 | 17 | N/A | 9-15  
Pond | 19 | 19 | 19 | 19 | 19 | 18-19 | 19 | 16-19  
Depression | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20 | 20  
      
    
    *   1 in 10 also includes **hills**
        aka Hill Forest Decid., Hill Forest Evrgr. in Worldographer.
    **  1 in 10 also includes **forest**
        aka Hill Forest Decid., Hill Forest Evrgr. in Worldographer.
    *** 1 in 20 have a **pass** which leads through the range
        aka Shapes->Preset: Trail->Curve, reduce Width, e.g. 5 click
        points through mountain to represent pass.
    

_Appendix B – Terrain Guide_

  * **Plain:** tundra, steppe, savanna, prairie, heath, moor, downs, meadow e.g. _Farmland_ in Worldographer
  * **Scrub:** brush, veldt, bush, thickets, brackens e.g. _Grassland_ in Worldographer
  * **Forest:** woods, jungle, groves and copses (light forest) e.g. _Forest Decid._ , _Forest Evrgr._ , etc. in Worldographer
  * **Rough:** badlands e.g. _Other Badland_ in Worldographer
  * **Desert:** barrens, waste, flat, snowfield e.g. _Desert Sandy_ in Worldographer
  * **Hills:** ridges, bluffs, dunes e.g. _Hills_ in Worldographer
  * **Mountains:** mesas, glacier, tors e.g. _Mtn_ in Worldographer
  * **Marsh:** fen, slough, swamp, bog, mire, quagmire, morass e.g. _Marsh_ in Worldographer
  * **Pond:** pools, tarn, lake e.g. _Cosmic Planet High Water Medium Temperature_ with Override Default Scale and Scale height independently set appropriately for size and shape of pond/lake in Worldographer
  * **Depression:** gorge, rift, valley, canyon e.g. _Symbol Crater_ with Color override, Override Default Scale, Scale height independently and Rotate (clockwise) set appropriately for size, color and direction of gorge in Worldographer

Source: DMG p173 APPENDIX B: RANDOM WILDERNESS TERRAIN

Can continue to build out map at this level, if desired.

## Select Sub-level Hex Terrain

Note: Sub-level = CONTINENT level in Worldographer.

Starting hex = Center hex of large hex, e.g. 40.24, and should have
village/town icon and label from Atlas-level

Here’s the steps to drill into the central hex at the Atlas-level to start
creating the map you can use to in the first few sessions for the players to
start their hex crawl:

  1. In Worldographer, change Level to CONTINENT
  2. Select 5 for _Number of Tiles_ then click **OK** , **OK**

  1. Remove overspill hexes by selecting the Blank terrain then clicking on unwanted hex or holding down left mouse button and moving over them (overspill is any not part of the 6 large hexes surrounding starting large hex)
  2. Add label at Continent Level with the text “6mi/hex”

## Generate Sub-level Hex Terrain

This follows the same process as generating terrain at the Atlas-level except
it is for 31 hexes this time.

Here’s the steps to generate the terrain for the times surrounding your
starting settlement:

  1. Roll a d20 31 times, noting down the result for each roll. These are the 31 terrain types surrounding your starting hex.
  2. Check first few hexes have some additional plains, e.g. low numbers, so it makes sence for a settlement like this and re-roll, if necessary, until terrain distribution feels right for what you have in mind for this area
  3. Define the terrain type for each roll using the table below by matching the result under your starting tile’s terrain column, i.e. Plains
  4. Apply the generated terrains to all the tiles representing the higher level Atlas tile radiating out from the starting hex, e.g. 40.25 
     * In Worldographer optionally blank out all hexes in center large hex except center starting hex to make it easier to see which hexes have had terrain from spreadsheet applied
     * Optionally make the center hex Farmland if village with farms
     * Apply randomly generated terrain to surrounding hexes until the terrain type starting at hex above starting hex. Proceed up until top of large hex reached, e.g. 40.42, 40.23, then proceed from hex to the right down to bottom of large hex, or until change in terrain type, e.g. 41.22, 41.23, 41.21, etc.
     * Repeat until all hexes adjacent hexes to center starting hex are filled: 
       * When change in terrain reached set that hex to the new terrain type then start over at hex below or to the right of starting hex, e.g. 40.26, and proceed to bottom of large hex then proceed from hex to left up to top of large hex, or until change in terrain type
       * When change in terrain reached set that hex to the new terrain type then start over hex at below or to the left starting hex
     * Now apply adhoc to remaining hexes using generated terrain as guidance, e.g. pick an unfilled hex to start applying the rest of the terrain to
     * Depressions & Ponds: retains prior terrain type and apply special marking indicating it’s a depression or pond
     * 1 in 10 chance for Hills to include Forests and Forests to include Hills: roll a d10 for each hill and each forest hex to see if they contain both then update hex to represent that (link in step 1 automatically does this for you)

## Generate Terrain

Starting Tile: Plains Scrub Forest Desert Hills Mountains Marsh Number of
Hexes: Rolls: Terrain Types:

Re-roll

* * *

# That's it, for now!

Check out the Blog for more posts!

  
  
\- Back to Top -

content.Title: Fine-Tuning LLMs: 3 Practical Approaches
content.Content: Fine-tuning LLMs is crucial for real-world applications. We do this by updating its internal settings\u200a—\u200athe parameters or weights of the model. If you’re training a model that’s already had some training, the activity is called “fine-tuning”.The purpose of fine-tuning is to teach the LLM to understand and follow a required chat or response format and to adapt the broad knowledge it was trained on to perform a specific task very well or to have specialized knowledge of a\xa0domain.When using datasets that are specially curated to train an LLM with instructions that have examples of requests and responses that have been validated to be what you want then this is know as supervised fine-tuning (SFT).Why Fine-Tune a\xa0Model?The following weaknesses of base models can be overcome with effective fine-tuning:Specialized domains: Most LLMs are not PhD level in all subject areas, but they are closing in and many recently released models even exceed PhD level. They also may not have had access to domain knowledge or propriety information during training that is required to accurately make the predictions that you\xa0require.Recent events: LLMs have limited knowledge beyond training cut-off data. Any LLM is trained, or fine-tuned, on a subset of the total world knowledge dataset so you have to constantly train your LLM to keep up with recent\xa0events.Can confidently make mistakes: General-purpose LLMs have many blindspots (aka hallucinations). If a chatbot without RAG is asked a question about something it wasn’t trained on, there is a high chance that it will give you a confident answer about something that isn’t\xa0true.If a general-purpose LLM by itself using techniques like multi-shot prompts, tools and/or retrieval augmented generation (RAG) isn’t providing the desired results then it may be time to fine-tune an LLM to meet your specific\xa0needs.Here’s how to do\xa0that.Training ApproachThe key is providing an instruction and answer dataset to train on. You refine an LLM’s capabilities using curated data in the form of pairs of instructions and corresponding answers.Many LLMs take in messages in the form of system, user and assistant “roles”:The system role (aka system prompt or system field) is used to define specific behaviors for the\xa0model.The user role (aka user prompt or instruction field) provides the necessary data (i.e. the concepts) and the task (e.g. constructing a sentence, estimating a price, creating a video title,\xa0etc.)The assistant role (aka output field) shows the expected answer that represents a high-quality response.To optimize a transformer type of neural network architecture like an LLM you usually use an adapter-based technique for efficiently fine-tuning models such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).Basically, you figure out the next token that your neural network predicted then compare it with what token should have been predicted to figure out how much you want to shift each of the different weights a little bit in order to make it better at predicting the correct token next\xa0time.LoRA steps:Freeze the Weights: initially you don’t optimize all the weights (8 billion in the case of Llama 3.1 8b) because it is too many knobs to turn, too many gradients.Target Modules: pick the layers (aka modules) that are the key for what you want to train. The target modules are the layers of the neural network that you will be focusing on for the purposes of training.Create Adaptor Matrices: The weights are frozen so instead create new matrices with lower dimensions aka Lower Rank, fewer parameters.Apply Adaptors to Target Modules: apply these matrices into the target modules so that they will adapt the target modules using a formula that use whatever values are in the Low Rank Adaptors to slightly shift what goes on in the target modules, i.e. they adapt\xa0them.The key metric used for improving LLM performance while training is measuring the difference between the predicted output and the true labels aka cross-entropy loss.The “Q” in QLoRA stands for Quantization which is a great trick that allows you to fit bigger models in memory with the same number of parameters just with lower precision. You lose some fine grained control over the weights so can’t adjust as precisely and some reduction in quality of the neural network but you don’t lose too much and still retains a lot of its\xa0power.For example:Llama 3.1 8B base model is 32,000\xa0MBWhen Quantized to 8 bit it is reduced to 9,000\xa0MBWhen Quantized to 4 bit it is reduced to 5,600\xa0MBWhen QLoRA r set to 32 it is reduced to 109\xa0MBThe four steps in training\xa0are:Forward pass: predict the next token in the training data, aka running inference.Loss calculation: how different was it to the correct next token, aka cross-entropy loss.Backward pass: how much should the parameters be tweaked to do better next time (the “gradients”), aka back propagation or backprop.Optimization: update parameters a tiny step to do better next\xa0time.HyperparametersHyperparamters are the knobs and switches data scientists use to control and tweak the training to make the model work better, or\xa0worse.The process of trying out different values is called hyperparameter optimization or hyperparameter tuning, which is just a fancy name for good old trial and\xa0error.By far the most impactful on getting the best results from your model is hyperparameter tuning where you wring every last drop out of your model to make it a little bit better at predicting outcomes. Improving the data quality of what goes in to the training is the easiest and most effective way to getting the most out of the\xa0model.The 5 important hyperparameters for the QLoRA fiune-tuning approach, the first 3 being the most essential for\xa0LoRA:r: the rank, or how many dimensions, in the low-rank matrices (aka lower dimensional adaptor matrix). Start with 8, then double to 16, then 32, until you see diminishing returns.Alpha: is the scaling factor used to multiply up the importance of this adaptor when it is applied to the target module, i.e. Alpha * LoRA_a matrix * LoRA_b matrix. Use twice the value of\xa0r.Target Modules: the layers of the neural network that are adapted. Target the attention head layers. See Model Layer Analysis below for more details on how to identify\xa0these.Quantization: reduce the precision of the weights in the base\xa0model.Dropout: a technique know as dropout regularization, which means it is a technique used to prevent the model from doing what is know as overfitting. Put simply, it removes a random subset of the neurons from the deep neural network, from the transformer. It takes a random percentage (say 10%) and wipes them out so the weights are discouraged from being too precise and looking too closely for a certain set of input\xa0tokens.5 important hyperparameters for training:Epochs: how many times are you going to go through your entire dataset as part of the training\xa0process.Batch Size: the number of training samples processed before the model’s parameters are\xa0updated.Learning Rates (LR): the step where you shift your weights in the next direction to do better next time. Typically its either 0.0001 or 0.00001. Using a cosine learning rate schedule means you start with LR that slowly decreases then decreases a lot then tails off at the end. Can use a warmup ratios too that at the very beginning of the training process when things are unstable because model has a lot to learn so dangerous to have a big LR initially this will start the training with a lower LR and warm it up to the peak LR then start cosine\xa0trailGradient Accumulation: allows you to improve the speed of going through training where you’d normally do a forward pass and get the loss then work out the gradients, going backwards, then take a step in the right direction, and repeat. Gradient Accumulation does a forward pass to get the gradients but doesn’t take a step. Instead you just take a second forward pass and get the gradients, add up those gradients and do that a few more times, i.e. keep accumulating these gradients, then take a step and optimize the neural\xa0network.Optimizer: is the formula that is used when it is time to make an update to your neural network to shift everything in the right direction so that next time it’s a bit more likely to predict the next token correctly. For example, Adam with Weight Decay has good convergence so does a good job of finding the optimal spot but comes at a cost of consuming a lot of memory because it keeps a rolling average of previous gradients.Model Layer\xa0AnalysisTo identify the target modules use AutoModelForCausalLM from the Hugging Face library to see the layers of your\xa0model.The core libraries you’ll need to analyze the neural network layers in your model\xa0are:transformers: Used to load the model and configure Quantization.torch: used in Quantization to specify the data type to use when in doing the calculations to improve performance.For example, looking at a Llama instruct model’s architecture and memory footprint:from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfigimport torch# Quantization allows you to use less memory when loading the modelquant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(    load_in_4bit=True, # What to reduce to, try 4 and 8 bit to compare accuracy    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, # To save more memory you can quantizes all of the weights twice    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, # Specifying the data type to use when in doing the calculations can improve performance    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4" # How to treat/interpret/compress numbers when reduced down to 4 or 8 bits, e.g. normalized float 4 bit (nf4))# Load quantized modelmodel = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", device_map="auto", quantization_config=quant_config)# View memory footprint of modelmemory = model.get_memory_footprint() / 1e6print(f"Model memory: {memory:,.1f} MB")# View neural network architecture layersmodelPyTorch layers of a Llama instruct\xa0model:LlamaForCausalLM(  (model): LlamaModel(    (embed_tokens): Embedding(128256, 4096)    (layers): ModuleList(      (0-31): 32 x LlamaDecoderLayer(        (self_attn): LlamaAttention(          (q_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=4096, bias=False)          (k_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=1024, bias=False)          (v_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=1024, bias=False)          (o_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=4096, bias=False)        )        (mlp): LlamaMLP(          (gate_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=14336, bias=False)          (up_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=4096, out_features=14336, bias=False)          (down_proj): Linear4bit(in_features=14336, out_features=4096, bias=False)          (act_fn): SiLU()        )        (input_layernorm): LlamaRMSNorm((4096,), eps=1e-05)        (post_attention_layernorm): LlamaRMSNorm((4096,), eps=1e-05)      )    )    (norm): LlamaRMSNorm((4096,), eps=1e-05)    (rotary_emb): LlamaRotaryEmbedding()  )  (lm_head): Linear(in_features=4096, out_features=128256, bias=False))The model is made up\xa0of:(embed_tokens): begins with embedding layer, which is how the tokens become embedded within the neural\xa0network(layers): next is a series of modules that are the layers within the neural network, including the tension layers that are at the heart of what makes a transformer (“attention is all you need”) and the multilayer perceptron (MLP) with an activation function, e.g. SiLU() the Sigmoid Linear Unit (SiLU) aka swish\xa0function(norm): the norm layer that implements the operation as described in the paper Layer Normalization(lm_head): the linear layer at the\xa0endAlways look at the dimensionality that are the number of input dimensions representing the vocab, e.g. Embedding(128256, 4096), and see that it matches the output, e.g. Linear(in_features=4096, out_features=128256, bias=False).The attention head layers in the Llama model can be found within the self_attn LlamaAttention layers of the neural network. Therefore, when fine-tuning a Llama base model the target modules should be: q_proj, v_proj, k_proj, and\xa0o_proj.Methods for Different Types of\xa0LLMsThere are several approaches you can take to fine-tuning LLMs depending on the type of LLM you’re fine-tuning (open source or a frontier model from OpenAI) and if a one-off training (like for a SLM used by an AI Agent) or if continues training (CT) is\xa0needed.Following is example code for first 2 situations and the third is a discussion on the pattern to use for\xa0CT:Fine-Tune a Frontier\xa0ModelFine-Tune an Open Source\xa0ModelContinuous Training (CT) using FTI ArchitectureMethod 1: Fine-Tune Frontier\xa0ModelYou may need to fine-tune a frontier model like one of OpenAIs models because you need\xa0to:Set the style or tone in a way that can’t be achieved with promptingImprove the reliability of producing a type of\xa0outputCorrect failures when using complex\xa0promptsHandle edge\xa0casesPerform a new skill or task that is hard to articulate in a\xa0promptThe three main states when fine-tuning with OpenAI\xa0are:Create a training dataset in jsonl format and upload to\xa0OpenAIRun training\u200a—\u200atraining loss and validation loss should\xa0decreaseEvaluate results, tweak and\xa0repeatYou’ll need to purchase from API tokens to run this. The minimum is $5 worth of credits, which is usually more than enough for multiple training runs. You’ll also need to create an API\xa0key.Dependencies and\xa0SetupThe core libraries you’ll need to fine-tune an OpenAI model\xa0are:json: for encoding and decoding between JSON and basic Python objects to create your training dataset in jsonl\xa0formatpickle: protocols for serializing and de-serializing a Python object structure so you can easily save and load your training\xa0datasetsopenai: use the OpenAI API SDK to upload training files and fine-tune specific OpenAI models like GPT 4o\xa0miniimport jsonimport picklefrom openai import OpenAIopenai_api_key = \'YOUR OPENAI API KEY\'openai = OpenAI()MODEL = \'gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18\'TRAIN_FILENAME = \'training-data.jsonl\'VALIDATION_FILENAME = \'validation-data.jsonl\'Load Curated\xa0DatasetsI recommend using pickle when doing one-off training locally on your machine or from notebooks to save your curated datasets so they can be quickly and easily loaded to fine-tune different models or the same model with different hyper parameters.OpenAI recommends fine-tuning with populations of 50–100 examples and it is a good practice to have both training and validation data. If you need additional training data Hugging Face has a good selection of general-purpose instruction datasets and those designed for particular tasks or\xa0domains.# Load in the training dataset:with open(\'your-training-filename.pkl\', \'rb\') as file:    train_file = pickle.load(file)train_dataset = train_file[:100]validation_dataset = train_file[100:150]Preparing the\xa0DataPrepare the data for fine-tuning in JSONL (JSON Lines) format and upload to\xa0OpenAI.Each row of JSON needs to contain message in the expected OpenAI prompt format. For\xa0example:{"messages" : [{"role": "system", "content": "System prompt"}, {"role": "user", "content": "User prompt"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Desired response"}]}{"messages" : [{"role": "system", "content": "System prompt"}, {"role": "user", "content": "User prompt"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Desired response"}]}{"messages" : [{"role": "system", "content": "System prompt"}, {"role": "user", "content": "User prompt"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Desired response"}]}Convert the items into jsonl and write them to a\xa0file.# Create JSONL from training dataset itemsdef create_jsonl(items):    result = ""    for item in items:        messages = [            {"role": "system", "content": "SYSTEM PROMPT define specific behaviors for the model, such as being helpful, always providing explanations, and tailoring responses as if speaking to a non technical user"},            {"role": "user", "content": "USER PROMPT based on item details, provide instructions or expected user inquiry"},            {"role": "assistant", "content": "RESPONSE TO COMPLETE with item answer included"}        ]        messages_str = json.dumps(messages)        result += \'{"messages": \' + messages_str +\'}\\n\'    return result.strip()# Write JSONL file to file system for future usedef write_jsonl_file(items, filename):    with open(filename, "w") as f:        jsonl = make_jsonl(items)        f.write(jsonl)write_jsonl_file(train_dataset, TRAIN_FILENAME)write_jsonl_file(validation_dataset, VALIDATION_FILENAME)Upload training and validation files to\xa0OpenAI:with open(TRAIN_FILENAME, "rb") as f:    train_file_uploaded = openai.files.create(file=f, purpose="fine-tune")with open(VALIDATION_FILENAME, "rb") as f:    validation_file_uploaded = openai.files.create(file=f, purpose="fine-tune")Monitor Fine-tuningOptionally monitor the fine-tuning with Weights & Biases (note: service accounts/keys are not available on the free tier but can test out with the free\xa0trial):Create a wandb project by logging in and from the dashboard click New project and enter a project\xa0nameRegister wandb key on OpenAI dashboard under Integrations on the General settings.Fine-tune ModelCreate an OpenAI fine-tuning job:wandb_project = {"type": "wandb", "wandb": {"project": "PROJECT NAME HERE"}}openai.fine_tuning.jobs.create(    training_file=train_file_uploaded.id,    validation_file=validation_file_uploaded.id,    model=MODEL,    seed=42,    hyperparameters={"n_epochs": 1}, # Try different values, more epochs for small training sets    integrations = [wandb_project], # Optionally use this    suffix="MODEL SUFFIX HERE" # Optionally inclue this in model name)# Monitor job progressopenai.fine_tuning.jobs.list(limit=1)# Get job IDjob_id = openai.fine_tuning.jobs.list(limit=1).data[0].id# Get more details on jobopenai.fine_tuning.jobs.retrieve(job_id)openai.fine_tuning.jobs.list_events(fine_tuning_job_id=job_id, limit=10).dataOpenAI will send an email notification once the job is completed and the name of your fine-tuned model. Here’s how you can get the name of the fine-tuned model in code from the job\xa0ID:# Get fine tuned model namefine_tuned_model_name = openai.fine_tuning.jobs.retrieve(job_id).fine_tuned_modelTest the Fine-tuned Modelresponse = openai.chat.completions.create(    model=fine_tuned_model_name,     messages=[        {"role": "system", "content": "SYSTEM PROMPT"},        {"role": "user", "content": "USER PROMPT"},        {"role": "assistant", "content": "RESPONSE TO COMPLETE without answer"}    ],    seed=42,    max_tokens=7 # Limit to number of tokens expected in response)reply = response.choices[0].message.contentMethod 2: Fine-Tune an Open Source\xa0ModelIf privacy is a concern and you need to host you own LLM then this is a great choice. With the right curated training dataset and hyperparameters you can even beat the frontier models for specific tasks or specialize domain of knowledge with this technique.Note: you’ll need somewhere to run this when not using one of the big AI company platforms like OpenAI so will take time and money. This example can run on Google Colab if you don’t own a computer with a GPU that has enough VRAM to run the model and train\xa0it.With a small dataset and a model that doesn’t need much memory you maybe able to use a T4 runtime and some purchased credits on the Pay As You Go plan but a medium to large dataset and any of the newer models with many parameters with need a more powerful GPU like an A100 that are only available with the Colab Pro\xa0plans.Dependencies and\xa0SetupThe core libraries you’ll need to fine-tune an open-source model available on Hugging Face\xa0are:huggingface_hub: allows you to login into HuggingFace, download and upload datasets and models from the\xa0hub.torch: used in Quantization to specify the data type to use when doing the calculations to improve performance.transformers: wrapper code around LLMs that follow the Transformer Architecture using either PyTorch or TensorFLow code. Used to load the tokenizer, load the model, and configure hyperparameters.datasets: used to access data repositories and load datasets on Hugging\xa0Face.wandb: used to monitor the progress of the fine-tuning process.peft: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (peft) utilities that allow you to train LLMs without having to work with all the billions of parameters in the LLMs. Used to pass in LoRA configurations.trl: Used to pass SFT configurations, execute the training, and create a response template, i.e. the chunk of text that is going to indicate that you to predict whatever comes\xa0next.from huggingface_hub import loginimport torchimport transformersfrom transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TrainingArguments, set_seed, BitsAndBytesConfigfrom datasets import load_dataset, Dataset, DatasetDictimport wandbfrom peft import LoraConfig, PeftModelfrom trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig, DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLMfrom datetime import datetimeBASE_MODEL = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B" # Choose from https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/modelsPROJECT_NAME = "YOUR NEW MODEL NAME HERE"HF_USER = "YOUR HUGGING FACE USERNAME HERE"DATASET_NAME = f"{HF_USER}/dataset-name-here" # To use your own or link to one from here: https://huggingface.co/datasetsMAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH = 182RUN_NAME =  f"{datetime.now():%Y-%m-%d_%H.%M.%S}"PROJECT_RUN_NAME = f"{PROJECT_NAME}-{RUN_NAME}"HUB_MODEL_NAME = f"{HF_USER}/{PROJECT_RUN_NAME}"# Hyperparameters for QLoRALORA_R = 32 # DimensionsLORA_ALPHA = 64 # Double rTARGET_MODULES = ["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj"] # Target modules of Llama architecture to trainLORA_DROPOUT = 0.1 # 10% of neurons removed from training setQUANT_4_BIT = True # Set to false to use 8 bit quantization# Hyperparameters for TrainingEPOCHS = 1 # Use more epochs if small datasetBATCH_SIZE = 4 # Set to 4 on T4 or 16 on A100 runtimeGRADIENT_ACCUMULATION_STEPS = 1 # Try 2 or 4 if having memory issuesLEARNING_RATE = 1e-4 # 1e-4 = 1 × 10^-4 = 0.0001LR_SCHEDULER_TYPE = \'cosine\' # Start with LR that slowly decreases then decreases a lot then tails off at the endWARMUP_RATIO = 0.03 # Start with a lower LR and warm it up to the peak LR then start cosine trailOPTIMIZER = "paged_adamw_32bit" # Adam with Weight Decay# Admin configSTEPS = 50 # Number of batch steps to take before it saves progress to wandbSAVE_STEPS = 5000 # How many steps before it uploads model to the hub# Log in to HuggingFacehf_token = \'YOUR HUGGING FACE TOKEN\'login(hf_token, add_to_git_credential=True)# Optional monitoring setup# Log in to Weights & Biaseswandb_api_key = userdata.get(\'WANDB_API_KEY\')os.environ["WANDB_API_KEY"] = wandb_api_keywandb.login()# Configure Weights & Biases to record against our projectos.environ["WANDB_PROJECT"] = PROJECT_NAMEos.environ["WANDB_LOG_MODEL"] = "checkpoint" if LOG_TO_WANDB else "end"os.environ["WANDB_WATCH"] = "gradients"wandb.init(project=PROJECT_NAME, name=RUN_NAME)Load Curated\xa0DatasetsThe quality of the data that you train your model on is a crucial factor, and a high number of samples is always desirable. Use about 100-10,000 for task-specific fine-tuning of small language models (SLMs) but much more samples will be needed for fine-tuning general-purpose LLMs, at least 1 million samples to create a good general-purpose instruct model and maybe as much for domain-specific models depending on the size of the domain (extent of its specialized knowledge and vocabulary).Below is an example of loading a dataset from Hugging Face. You can also save your datasets to Hugging Face to make them easy to share and load for training.# Load dataset from Hugging Facedataset = load_dataset(DATASET_NAME)training_dataset = dataset[\'train\']Load Tokenizer and the Base\xa0Model# Use 4 bit or 8 bit Quantizationif QUANT_4_BIT:  quant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(    load_in_4bit=True,    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"  )else:  quant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(    load_in_8bit=True,    bnb_8bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16  )# Load the Tokenizertokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL, trust_remote_code=True)tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_tokentokenizer.padding_side = "right"# Load the Modelbase_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(    BASE_MODEL,    quantization_config=quant_config,    device_map="auto",)base_model.generation_config.pad_token_id = tokenizer.pad_token_idCheck how much memory is used loading the\xa0model:print(f"Base model memory: {base_model.get_memory_footprint() / 1e6:.1f} MB")Response TemplateYou don’t may not want your model to learn about how to predict all of the tokens of the prompt up until the answer you expect so don’t have it spending lots of time seeing how good it is at writing descriptions and explanations. Your may want to to focus on a specific answer based on the instruct\xa0field.Therefore, set up a mask (aka data collator or response template) so that when you tell the trainer that you don’t need it to learn about the prompt you just want it to take it into account to provide it context but to learn how to predict this token right here after what’s in the provided template.The HuggingFace DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM helper class tis a simple utility that allows you to do\xa0this:Come up with response template for the text that is going to indicate that you want it to predict whatever comes\xa0nextThen create an instance using response template and tokenizerresponse_template = "RESPONSE TO COMPLETE without answer"collator = DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM(response_template, tokenizer=tokenizer)Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) Trainer ConfigurationsPass in LoRA and SFT configurations, pulled from constants in setup. The hardcoded configurations are hyperparameters that don’t matter and should always stay the\xa0same.# LoRA configurationlora_config = LoraConfig(    lora_alpha=LORA_ALPHA,    lora_dropout=LORA_DROPOUT,    r=LORA_R,    bias="none",    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",    target_modules=TARGET_MODULES,)# Training configurationtraining_config = SFTConfig(    output_dir=PROJECT_RUN_NAME,    num_train_epochs=EPOCHS,    per_device_train_batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,    per_device_eval_batch_size=1,    eval_strategy="no", # Best practice is to use an evaluation strategy by passing in validation data and well as training data    gradient_accumulation_steps=GRADIENT_ACCUMULATION_STEPS,    optim=OPTIMIZER,    save_steps=SAVE_STEPS,    save_total_limit=10,    logging_steps=STEPS,    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,    weight_decay=0.001,    fp16=False,    bf16=True,    max_grad_norm=0.3,    max_steps=-1,    warmup_ratio=WARMUP_RATIO,    group_by_length=True,    lr_scheduler_type=LR_SCHEDULER_TYPE,    report_to="wandb",    run_name=RUN_NAME,    max_seq_length=MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH,    dataset_text_field="text",    save_strategy="steps",    hub_strategy="every_save", # Push to the hub every time that it is doing a save    push_to_hub=True,    hub_model_id=HUB_MODEL_NAME,    hub_private_repo=True # Make it a private repo)Setup SFTTrainer by passing\xa0in:The base model to train, e.g. Llama 3.1\xa08BTraining data to\xa0useLoRA parametersTraining parametersThe collator to tell it to focus on predicting whatever comes after your response\xa0template# Supervised Fine Tuning Trainer configurationsft_trainer = SFTTrainer(    model=base_model,    train_dataset=training_dataset,    peft_config=lora_config,    args=training_config,    data_collator=collator  )Fine-tune ModelTrain the model and save to the hub after training the model then stop the monitoring, if\xa0used:sft_trainer.train()# Push fine-tuned model to Hugging Facesft_trainer.model.push_to_hub(PROJECT_RUN_NAME, private=True)# if monitoring with wandb run this once completedwandb.finish()Note: this could take several days or a week to complete depending on the size of your dataset and chosen runtime. Make sure you have purchased enough credits for\xa0this.Test the Fine-tuned ModelUse the model in inference mode, i.e.\xa0.generate() instead of\xa0.train().fine_tuned_model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, HUB_MODEL_NAME)set_seed(42)inputs = tokenizer.encode("TEST PROMPT HERE", return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")attention_mask = torch.ones(inputs.shape, device="cuda")outputs = fine_tuned_model.generate(inputs, attention_mask=attention_mask, max_new_tokens=3, num_return_sequences=1)response = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0])Method 3: Continuous Training (CT) using FTI ArchitectureThe previous 2 methods can be used for this, however, the approach when constantly training a model is different and is more in line with traditional data engineering.The key to CT is to create a reliable set of data collection pipelines that that uses extract-transform load (ETL) to store the raw data in a data warehouse for downstream systems like data analytics, machine learning (ML), and fine-tuning LLMs.A feature pipeline then takes raw data as input, processes it, and saves the “features” and “labels” required by the model for training or inference in a feature store (usually a vector database).Then a training pipeline is used the cleaned data from the feature store as inputs to fine-tune LLMs and creates a trained model that are stored in the model registry.You can then use an inference pipeline that takes as input the features and labels from the feature store and the trained model from the model registry to make predictions by querying the vector DB for chunked documents, reports, messages, etc. for\xa0RAG.Versioning the features and labels is important in CT so you can can always ensure at that the training and inference time features match and avoid the training-serving skew problem and will always know what data the model was trained on. Also, versioning the features, labels, and models means you can easily upgrade or roll back the deployment of the\xa0model.This approach is known as the FTI\xa0pattern.ConclusionFine-tuning models is expensive and time consuming so you should explore alternatives first like developing a non-AI software solution, traditional ML, or using RAG first to see if it meets your\xa0needs.SFT is great when privacy is needed or the data needed just isn’t publicly available to train the popular LLMs on so you need run your own open-source LLM for a specific task or domain that can be trained to perform better with less operational costs than a model with lots of parameters and prevent hallucinations when making predictions on subjects missing from the original training\xa0dataset.If your business or social media platforms are continuously generating new data and your LLM needs to always have the latest information at inference time then you’ll need to consider setting up CTCICD (continuous training, continuous integration and continuous deliver) following best data and ML engineering practices.Please let me know if interested in more examples of SFT such as other frontier models, languages, specific libraries or frameworks. Also, if interested in how to implement the various FTI pipelines or\xa0RAG.

content.Title: Hugging Face Launch Open Source Programmable Robot!
content.Content: Games like Skyrim and 7 Days to Die changed how we gamers and the gaming industry approached gaming by opening them up to the community for\xa0modding.This provided endless opportunities for us to customize the games we play with our friends to our unique gaming group and now we can do the same with\xa0robots!Reachy Mini Robot from Hugging\xa0FaceReachy MiniFor under 300 bucks you can to buy a desktop robot from Hugging Face that sits next to your keyboard plugged into your computer.Out-of-the-box this 11 inch tall robot wiggles, twitches antenna at you, tracks your face, and even dances. It supports vision, text and speech that you can train your AI model to interpret, make decisions based on what it sees and hears, hold conversations, and interact with its surroundings.The best thing about this robot is that it is completely open source so we can modify it’s behavior and share it with the community creating endless possibilities.What makes it open source? Well, it can use open source AI models and it uses fully open-source and community-supported hardware, software, and simulation environments.Your innovations can be put up on GitHub so you, me, your kids, and anyone that knows a bit of Python, JavaScript or Scratch can program it, teaching it new tricks, and share your code (aka Motion Packs) so we can build on each others creativity.For example, there is already a Reachy Mini motor controller by Pollen Labs available on GitHub and several projects on the Reachy Hugging Face\xa0Space.There is also a version that’s for a $150 more comes with a Raspberry Pi, battery, wifi, 4 microphones, and an accelerometer that lets Reachy Mini freely roam around the house untethered to chase the dog and annoy the\xa0cats.Type 1 Kardashev Civilization Here We\xa0Come!K-Scale Labs are on a mission to help the world build billions of general-purpose robots from home by making them open-source and universally accessible.They want to help us build our own humanoid robotics without having to really on or trust closed source, giant tech and car companies to create them for us or charge us an arm and a leg to have them in our\xa0homes.The key is choosing the right components like actuators and gearboxes in additional to providing open source code and all the CAD models with the community.They’re a small team working out of their garage building, experimenting and iterating on bringing this technology to all of us, iterating on the components needed to build robots to make them affordable.Meet KBot, your personal, open source, full stack robot in your hands that you can teach to help around the house, wash the dishes, cook dinner, and make you a good cup of\xa0tea.Please share your home robot builds and any mods you create with the community.

content.Title: 7 Steps to Building and Training Effective SLMs
content.Content: Fine-tuning open-source LLM and monitoring cross entropy\xa0lossSmall Language Models (SLMs) are fast becoming the best choice for many Generative AI use cases, especially Agentic\xa0AI.Nvidia wrote the paper Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI that said they\xa0are:…sufficiently powerful, inherently more suitable, and necessarily more economical for many invocations in agentic systems, and are therefore the future of agentic\xa0AI.But why are they more suitable and how to you build\xa0them?Why Use an\xa0SLM?One of the major reasons is that they’re more cost effective than running your own open-source Large Language Model\xa0(LLM).However, with the cost effectiveness of powerful, frontier models like GPT, Claude, Gemini, etc. that are significantly cheaper and, in most cases, faster than any LLMs you can run on your own due to economies of scale are there other reasons for using\xa0them?Privacy\u200a—\u200ayou need to augment or fine-tune your LLM with data not available to OpenAI or Google like customer account information, proprietary product information, company policies and procedures, financial reports, or other data that prevents you from using a closed source LLM or running your model anywhere except on-prem to comply with industry regulations such as GDPR,\xa0HIPAA.Old Data\u200a—\u200adepending on the knowledge cut-off date and what subset of data available in the world was used it may not have the latest information required or you may need to continuously train it on new data as it is generated.Cost\u200a—\u200aRunning foundation open-source LLMs with many parameters is expensive due to their memory and processing requirements, especially to train the entire model and when used by a lot of\xa0users.Hallucinations\u200a—\u200aWhen an LLM is asked about something that wasn’t in its training dataset it can confidently give you an answer that isn’t true which can ruin any confidence users have in your solution.Better Results\u200a—\u200ain some cases a fine-tuned SLM can actually perform better than a frontier model, non-AI software solutions, and traditional machine learning\xa0(ML).Building SLMsOK, so how would you go about creating an SML? In a nutshell, you train it, or, more correctly, fine-tune it and use techniques like quantization to reduce it in\xa0size.To do that effectively you need to approach it like most engineering problems with a well defined process to ensure it solves the problem, is reliable, scales and is worth the cost compared to other solutions.Use these steps to build an\xa0SLM:Define the\xa0ProblemData CurationBuild baselines for\xa0NLPSelect the right base\xa0modelFine-tune the selected\xa0model(s)Evaluate your fine-tuned modelSelect the tech stack for your\xa0SLMStep 1: Define the\xa0ProblemLike traditional software engineering when building a solution you really need to understand the problem you are trying to solve and why it needs solving. That involves all the usual suspects:Requirements gathering and\xa0analysisFunctional and non-functional requirementsMetrics for measuring the success of the\xa0projectHow will you evaluate performance?You need to define the key performance indicators (KPIs) so you know if your GenAI solution solves the problem and is worth investing in building or not. There’s not much point if a software solution already exists or well-established, traditional ML technique solves the problem better than your AI and is cheaper and/or quicker to implement.Model-centric or technical metric:Training loss\u200a—\u200ameasures based on cross-entropy lossValidation loss\u200a—\u200asame measure as training loss but with the validation datasetPerplexity\u200a—\u200ameasure the exponential of the cross-entropy loss, the lower the\xa0betterGradient norm\u200a—\u200aduring training use tools to monitor gradients to detect vanishing gradients, exploding gradients or instabilityRegression problems\u200a—\u200aRoot Mean Squared Log Error\xa0(RMSLE)Other metrics\u200a—\u200athis depends on the problem you’re trying to\xa0solveBusiness-centric or outcome metrics should be simple and understandable by humans to measure the success and value against other approaches. Work with the project sponsor, business analysts, subject matter experts (SMEs), and end users to identify\xa0these.Create a criteria used to judge if the estimate/result is of good quality then measure what percent of the model’s results meet this criteria so they can be compared across solutions.Step 2: Data\xa0CurationSelect, curate and craft a dataset that is balanced to test baseline models for comparison with your fine-tuned model. You can find datasets on HuggingFace or provide your own data available within your organization.Begin by scrubbing and curating the chosen dataset by first focusing on a subset of the data then scale it up and apply it to the full\xa0dataset.Data curation:Investigate the chosen dataset to verify suitability: review datapoints to determine if enough for training, validation, and testing (e.g. plot the distribution of certain data points in a bar chart, scatter graph and/or pie\xa0chart)Remove outliers from training\xa0datasetCreate a prompt to use for training by providing the answer during training and the same prompt without the answer that the model will learn to\xa0completePlot the distribution of token counts for all the prompts generated from the training dataset to ensure they’re not too short (discard these if not enough information) or too long (truncate them to an appropriate length)\u200a—\u200athis is an example of a hyperparameter you can adjust and experiment with for the best\xa0resultsSplit the dataset into a training, test and validation datasetSave in a dataset repository and make available to\xa0useData curation is an important skill for LLM engineers and data scientists to learn, so that you can build solutions with high quality datasets to get the best\xa0results.Step 3: Build Baselines for\xa0NLPIdentify the various solutions to the problem you’re trying to solve and use the test dataset to quickly see how well they do, documenting the results to compare with each other and your fine-tuned model.For example, create a bar chart with your core metric for comparing each of the solutions tested, such as traditional ML techniques (feature engineering, linear regression, bag of words, random forest, etc.) using various approaches to natural language processing (NLP) to generate vectors (like Word2vec, BERT, etc.), a human expert making educated guesses, and various frontier\xa0models.You can use free vector embeddings like the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model available in the sentence-transformers Python framework and compare embedding models on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) leaderboard.Step 4: Select the Right Base\xa0ModelUse the various leader boards and arenas comparing LLMs to help choose the right\xa0model:HuggingFace leaderboards\u200a—\u200ae.g. Open LLM, the Old Open LLM board,BigCode, LLM Perf,\xa0etc.Vellum\u200a—\u200ahas comparison tools and\xa0graphsSEAL\u200a—\u200aexpert\xa0skillsLMSYS Chatbot Arena\u200a—\u200acompares frontier and open-source models directly using blind human evals based on head-to-head comparison measured with an Elo\xa0ratingUse various benchmarks:Knowledge\u200a—\u200aMassive Multi-Task Language Understanding (MMLU)Reasoning\u200a—\u200aHellaSwag, ARC-C, Winogrande, PIQAThe best model depends on your requirements and specific use case. Compare the following features of the LLM to find the best\xa0fit:Open-source or\xa0ClosedRelease date and knowledge cut-offParametersTraining tokensContext lengthInference cost: API charge (credits/cost per 1M input & output tokens), Subscription or Runtime\xa0computeTraining costBuild costTime to\xa0MarketRate limits (stability)SpeedLatencyLicensePrivacySecurityEvaluating the models is essential for selecting the most relevant LLM and making sure fine-tuning it will actually improve the\xa0model.For a SLM you’ll want a base model that already works reasonably well for your problem and doesn’t have too many parameters. You then use various techniques to reduce the size of it (e.g. quantization) and target specific areas of the neural network to fine-tune (e.g. LoRA) rather than training the whole\xa0model.Step 5: Fine-Tune the Selected\xa0Model(s)You’ll need to decide on your training approach, what hyperparameters to experiment with, where to host your open-source LLM, what experiment tracker to use, and where to run the training.Training ApproachDetermine the training approach to use such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PERF) and QLoRA. The four steps in QLoRA training\xa0are:Forward pass— predict the next token in the training data, aka running inferenceLoss calculation— how different was it to the true next token, aka cross-entropy lossBackward pass— how much should we tweak parameters to do better next time (the “gradients”), aka back propagation or\xa0backpropOptimization— update parameters a tiny step to do better next\xa0timeHyperparametersImportant hyper-parameters for training that you should experiment with and adjust on different training runs (make sure you document what you used each time so you have reproducible training results and know what combination worked\xa0best):Epochs\u200a—\u200ahow many times are you going to go through your entire dataset as part of the training\xa0processBatch Size\u200a—\u200adepends on where you’re running the training, e.g. if on Google Colab then on a T4 runtime it can probably handle running 4 batches whereas on an A100 box this can go up to\xa016Learning Rates —that step size where you shift your weights in the next direction to do better next\xa0timeGradient Accumulation\u200a—\u200aa technique that allows you to improve the speed of going through\xa0trainingOptimizer\u200a—\u200athe process/algorithm that is used when it is time to make an update to your neural network to shift everything a little bit in a good direction so that next time it’s a bit more likely to predict the next token correctlyFine-tuningTo fine-tune your model you’ll need\xa0to:Load your curated\xa0datasetsPrepare the data for training, e.g. fine-tuning GPT requires it to be in JSONL (JSON Lines) format and uploaded to OpenAI, save on HuggingFace hub, or use pickle to save it\xa0locallyRun you’re fine-tuning and monitor it’s progress with an experiment trackerRepeat with different models and hyperparametersStep 6: Evaluate Your Fine-Tuned ModelDeploy your fine-tuned model with an inference endpoint and evaluate it with your test dataset recording the same metrics used when testing the baselines for comparison (update your bar chart comparing the core metrics of your baselines and fine-tuned model).Repeat steps 4 and 5 until you have a model that doesn’t require a lot of memory to run but performs as good, or even better, than the frontier models and outperforms the base open source models with a large number of parameters.Step 7: Select the Tech Stack for Your\xa0SLMOpen-source LLMs are free so are obviously cheaper than a fancy, trillion parameter frontier model, right? Well, no. The large companies have invested billions to train their LLMs, they spread their costs over many users (better rates on compute due to economies of scale and a good deal with Microsoft and Nvidia) plus they’re subsidized by venture capital so can keep token costs artificially low (at least until the AI bubble\xa0bursts).ComputeTraining and running your own model needs compute and\xa0memory:Data
